title: The History of Tea
passage:
Tea is one of the most widely consumed beverages in the world, second only to water. According to legend, tea was discovered in 2737 BCE by the Chinese Emperor Shen Nung, when leaves from a wild tree blew into his pot of boiling water. For centuries tea remained a distinctly Chinese product, valued both as a medicine and as a refreshing drink.

Tea reached Europe in the seventeenth century through Dutch and Portuguese traders. In Britain it was initially an expensive luxury, taxed heavily by the government, which made it a symbol of wealth. It was not until the nineteenth century, when large plantations were established in India and Sri Lanka, that prices fell far enough for tea to become an everyday drink for ordinary people.

Today tea is grown in more than forty countries, and each region produces leaves with a distinctive character shaped by soil, altitude and climate. The process of turning fresh leaves into the dried product involves withering, rolling, oxidising and drying — and small variations in these steps create the difference between green, black and oolong teas.

questions.q: According to the passage, which drink is consumed more than tea?
questions.explanation: The first sentence says tea is 'second only to water'.

questions.q: Tea became a cheap, everyday drink in Britain as soon as it arrived in the 17th century.
questions.explanation: It was an expensive luxury; prices only fell in the 19th century.

questions.q: Complete the sentence: Large tea plantations were established in India and ____ in the nineteenth century.
questions.explanation: The passage names India and Sri Lanka.

questions.q: What creates the difference between green, black and oolong tea?
questions.explanation: Small variations in withering, rolling, oxidising and drying create the differences.

questions.q: Shen Nung wrote a book describing the health benefits of tea.
questions.explanation: The passage mentions the legend of his discovery but says nothing about him writing a book.

title: Urban Green Spaces
passage:
As cities grow, planners increasingly recognise the value of parks, gardens and other green spaces. Beyond their obvious recreational appeal, these areas provide measurable environmental benefits. Trees and plants absorb carbon dioxide and release oxygen, while their leaves trap airborne particles that would otherwise harm human health.

Green spaces also help cities cope with heat. Dense concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight and re-radiate it, producing the so-called 'urban heat island' effect, which can make city centres several degrees warmer than surrounding countryside. Vegetation counteracts this by providing shade and by cooling the air as water evaporates from leaves.

Research further suggests that access to nature improves mental well-being, reducing stress and encouraging physical activity. For these reasons many modern city plans now set targets for the amount of green space that must be available within walking distance of every home.

questions.q: What causes the 'urban heat island' effect?
options: Concrete and asphalt absorbing and re-radiating heat
questions.explanation: Dense concrete and asphalt absorb sunlight and re-radiate it.

questions.q: The passage claims green spaces can improve people's mental well-being.
questions.explanation: Research suggests access to nature reduces stress and improves well-being.

questions.q: Complete: Vegetation cools the air as water ____ from leaves.
questions.explanation: The passage says the air is cooled as water evaporates from leaves.

questions.q: Most cities have already met their green space targets.
questions.explanation: The passage says plans set targets, but never states whether cities have met them.

title: The Rise of Remote Work
passage:
The idea of working away from a central office is far older than the internet. In the 1970s, an American engineer named Jack Nilles coined the term 'telecommuting' after realising that the fuel consumed by commuters might be saved if information, rather than people, were made to travel. His proposal attracted modest interest, but the technology of the era — expensive terminals and slow telephone lines — kept the practice marginal.

What changed the picture was not a single invention but the steady accumulation of cheap bandwidth, portable computers and, crucially, software that allowed documents to be edited by several people at once. By the 2010s a minority of employees in knowledge-based industries were already working remotely for part of the week. The disruption of 2020 then compressed a decade of gradual adoption into a matter of months, as organisations that had insisted remote work was impractical implemented it within weeks.

The consequences remain contested. Employers point to reduced office costs and access to a wider pool of applicants, while noting concerns about the erosion of informal mentoring, which tends to happen through overheard conversation rather than scheduled meetings. Employees, for their part, consistently report valuing the recovered commuting time above almost every other benefit. What most researchers now expect is neither a full return to the office nor its disappearance, but a hybrid arrangement whose exact shape is still being negotiated workplace by workplace.

questions.q: Which term did Jack Nilles invent in the 1970s?
questions.explanation: The passage states he coined the term 'telecommuting'.

questions.q: Why did telecommuting remain uncommon in the 1970s?
options: Employers had not heard of the idea
The available technology was costly and slow
questions.explanation: Expensive terminals and slow telephone lines kept the practice marginal.

questions.q: The events of 2020 accelerated a trend that was already under way.
questions.explanation: It 'compressed a decade of gradual adoption into a matter of months'.

questions.q: Remote workers in 2020 were paid less than office-based colleagues.
questions.explanation: Pay is never discussed anywhere in the passage.

questions.q: Does the writer believe offices will disappear completely?
questions.explanation: The writer expects 'neither a full return to the office nor its disappearance', but a hybrid arrangement.

questions.q: According to the passage, informal mentoring usually occurs through:
questions.explanation: It 'tends to happen through overheard conversation rather than scheduled meetings'.

title: Coral Reefs Under Threat
passage:
Coral reefs occupy less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they shelter roughly a quarter of all marine species. This extraordinary density of life rests on an unlikely partnership. The coral animal, a soft polyp that builds a hard limestone skeleton, houses microscopic algae called zooxanthellae within its tissues. The algae photosynthesise and pass as much as ninety per cent of the sugars they produce to their host; in return they receive shelter and a reliable supply of nutrients.

This partnership is finely tuned to temperature, and therein lies its vulnerability. When water grows too warm for too long, the algae begin producing compounds that damage the polyp, which responds by expelling them. The coral loses its colour — a phenomenon known as bleaching — and, more importantly, its main source of food. A bleached coral is not dead, and if temperatures fall quickly enough the algae can be reacquired. If the heat persists, however, the polyp starves.

Warming is not the only pressure. As the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide it becomes more acidic, which slows the rate at which corals can deposit their skeletons. Locally, sediment from coastal construction clouds the water and blocks the light the algae require. Efforts at restoration have shown some promise: fragments of heat-tolerant coral can be grown in nurseries and transplanted onto degraded reefs. Yet marine biologists are careful to describe such work as buying time rather than providing a solution, since none of it addresses the temperature of the ocean itself.

questions.q: What is the name of the algae that live inside coral tissues?
questions.explanation: The passage names the microscopic algae as zooxanthellae.

questions.q: What proportion of the sugars produced by the algae goes to the coral?
options: As much as ninety per cent
questions.explanation: The algae 'pass as much as ninety per cent of the sugars they produce to their host'.

questions.q: A coral that has bleached is already dead.
questions.explanation: The passage explicitly says 'a bleached coral is not dead' and may recover.

questions.q: Ocean ____ slows the rate at which corals build their skeletons. (one word)
questions.explanation: As the ocean absorbs CO2 it becomes more acidic — ocean acidification.

questions.q: Does the writer think coral nurseries solve the underlying problem?
questions.explanation: Such work 'buys time rather than providing a solution', as it does not address ocean temperature.

questions.q: Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the first sentence.

title: The Science of Sleep
passage:
For most of the twentieth century sleep was regarded as a passive state — the brain, like a machine at the end of a shift, simply switching off. The invention of the electroencephalogram overturned this assumption. Recordings revealed that the sleeping brain passes through repeated cycles of distinct stages, some of which show electrical activity as vigorous as that of waking.

A full cycle lasts roughly ninety minutes and moves from light sleep into deep, slow-wave sleep and then into a paradoxical phase characterised by rapid eye movement, or REM. The proportions shift across the night: slow-wave sleep dominates the early cycles, while REM periods lengthen towards morning. Each phase appears to serve different functions. Slow-wave sleep is associated with physical restoration and with the consolidation of factual memory, whereas REM has been linked to emotional regulation and to the kind of associative thinking that underlies creative insight.

More recent work has identified a further role. During deep sleep the spaces between brain cells expand, allowing cerebrospinal fluid to flush through the tissue and carry away metabolic waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Among these is beta-amyloid, a protein whose build-up is a hallmark of Alzheimer's disease. The finding has reframed chronic sleep deprivation as a possible risk factor rather than merely an unpleasant condition — though researchers caution that the direction of causation has yet to be established firmly, since poor sleep may equally be an early symptom of the disease process.

questions.q: What overturned the belief that sleep is a passive state?
questions.explanation: The invention of the EEG revealed cycles of active brain states.

questions.q: Approximately how many minutes does one full sleep cycle last?
questions.explanation: A full cycle lasts roughly ninety minutes.

questions.q: Which phase becomes longer towards the morning?
questions.explanation: REM periods lengthen towards morning.

questions.q: Slow-wave sleep is linked to the consolidation of factual memory.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the second paragraph.

questions.q: During deep sleep, cerebrospinal fluid removes metabolic ____ from brain tissue.
questions.explanation: The fluid carries away metabolic waste products.

questions.q: Is the writer certain that poor sleep causes Alzheimer's disease?
questions.explanation: Researchers caution the direction of causation is not firmly established; poor sleep may be a symptom.

title: The Printing Press and the Spread of Ideas
passage:
When Johannes Gutenberg assembled his printing press in Mainz around 1450, he combined existing elements — the screw press already used for wine, oil-based inks, and the concept of movable type known in Asia for centuries — into a system suited to the European alphabet. His genius lay less in any single component than in the metal alloy he devised for casting type, which was durable enough to survive thousands of impressions yet melted at a low enough temperature to be recast easily.

The consequences were swift and disproportionate. Within fifty years presses were operating in more than two hundred European cities, and the price of a book had fallen so far that a scholar could own a personal library rather than travelling to consult a chained manuscript. Standardisation followed: because every copy from a print run was identical, scholars in different countries could for the first time refer to the same page of the same edition, a precondition for the cumulative verification that characterises modern science.

Historians have nevertheless warned against attributing too much to the machine alone. Printing amplified whatever was already circulating, and it served polemic as readily as scholarship — the religious conflicts of the sixteenth century were fought in cheap pamphlets as much as in pulpits. What the press altered was not the character of ideas but the speed and scale at which they could travel, and that shift was sufficient to make institutions built on controlling the copying of texts suddenly fragile.

questions.q: According to the passage, Gutenberg's most important innovation was:
options: The metal alloy used for casting type
questions.explanation: His genius 'lay less in any single component than in the metal alloy he devised for casting type'.

questions.q: Movable type was invented in Europe.
questions.explanation: The concept was 'known in Asia for centuries' before Gutenberg.

questions.q: Within fifty years, presses were operating in more than ____ European cities.
questions.explanation: The passage says more than two hundred European cities.

questions.q: Why was the standardisation of printed copies important for science?
options: It made books cheaper to produce
It allowed scholars to refer to the same page of the same edition
It reduced the number of printing errors to zero
questions.explanation: Identical copies let scholars in different countries cite the same page — a precondition for cumulative verification.

questions.q: Does the writer agree that the printing press alone explains the changes of the period?
questions.explanation: Historians warn 'against attributing too much to the machine alone'; it amplified what already circulated.

questions.q: Gutenberg became wealthy from his invention.
questions.explanation: The passage never discusses Gutenberg's personal finances.
